opus-5.5.text:
I think, honestly, it started with curiosity more than any grand plan. When I was in middle school, computers felt a bit like magic: you could type something in and the machine would actually do what you told it. That sense of being able to create something from nothing, just with logic and a keyboard, was really exciting to me.

I remember getting into programming through small things at first. You write a little program, maybe something that solves a math problem or draws something on the screen, and when it works there's this immediate feedback. You see the result right away. And when it doesn't work, you have to figure out why, which is like a puzzle. I enjoyed that loop a lot: try something, fail, debug, and finally get it right.

I think what also drew me in was that it felt very open-ended. In a lot of subjects at school, there's a fixed answer you're supposed to get. With computers, there were many ways to solve the same problem, and you could keep making things better, faster, cleaner. That idea of building tools and systems, rather than just finding answers, stuck with me. In some ways it's the same thing I still enjoy today, just at a much bigger scale.

r001.rationale: The response describes curiosity, programming experiments, and debugging, but does not mention an ambition to make web pages or a teacher giving him an introductory C programming book.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it started with games. My family got a computer when I was in middle school, and like most kids I just wanted to play on it. But at some point I got curious about how the games actually worked, and that curiosity turned out to be stronger than the games themselves.

I remember getting hold of a book on programming, I think it was Pascal, and typing in little programs that would draw shapes or make a character move on the screen. The thing that hooked me was the feedback loop. You write something, you run it, and the machine does exactly what you told it, including the mistakes. That felt like magic and also very fair. The computer doesn't care who you are, it just executes your logic.

There was also the competitive side. In China at that time, informatics olympiad was a big thing, so I started doing algorithm problems. That gave me a reason to go deeper than just hacking around. You had to understand why something was fast or slow, not just whether it worked. I think that early habit of caring about efficiency stayed with me, and in hindsight it's basically what I still do today, trying to make computation go faster.

r001.rationale: The response mentions a Pascal programming book and curiosity about games, but does not describe wanting to make web pages or a teacher giving him an introductory C book.
